extracted.intended_audience: attorneys, legal officers, and federal officials responsible for custody, transfer, disposal, or acquisition of United States government property (esp. War Department/Army)
extracted.subtask_description: Compilation of legal standards and precedents governing disposition, transfer, loan, acceptance, purchase, custody, and accountability of United States public property, principally in the context of the War Department and military reservations. Includes when Congressional authority is required, exceptions in emergencies, and procedural duties of officers and boards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional authority required to dispose of public property
rubrics_metrics.description: No executive department or officer can dispose of public property of the United States except by the authority of Congress; the Constitution vests Congress with the power to 'dispose of and make all needful rules and regulations respecting the territory or other property belonging to the United States.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leading case: United States v. Nicoll (Fed. Cas. 15879) — sale or loan of public property by a commandant was illegal without authority; applies to sales, transfers, exchanges, and other dispositions unless Congress has explicitly authorized. Numerous decisions and Attorney General opinions cited reinforcing principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional rule applies equally to personalty and realty
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitutional provision regarding disposition of public property applies to personal property as well as to real property; executive officers cannot dispose of personalty absent Congressional authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that Secretary of War could not, in absence of enabling legislation, sell or negotiate bonds or promissory notes, nor alienate telegraph lines acquired by treaty (Porto Rico examples). Cases and Comptroller/Attorney General decisions cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: usufructuary grant vs. revocable license
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear distinction exists between granting a usufructuary interest in land (transfer of an interest) and issuing a revocable license which does not transfer such an interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secretary of War may permit revocable licenses (e.g., telegraph posts/wires removable at government's will; municipal water pipes or post-trader buildings subject to removal), but may not grant exclusive or permanent usufructuary rights (e.g., permanent ferry franchise, permanent bridge with easement, exclusive right to mine or exploit water power) without authority. Multiple decisions exemplify permissible licenses versus forbidden grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive cannot create permanent/exclusive franchises on military reservations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of War (or other executive officer) is not empowered to accede to applications that would create permanent, exclusive franchises or transfers of property interests in military reservations without Congressional authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: refusal to permit establishment of a ferry granting exclusive usufruct and toll-charging; refusal to permit permanent bridge involving easement; refusal to grant exclusive privilege to bore for gas and pipe it away. Cases: R. 38, 564; R. 42, 167; C. 285.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exchange of public property requires Congressional authority (with narrow exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: An exchange of public property for other property not belonging to the United States cannot be made except by authority of Congress; exchanges are governed by statutory constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where statutes authorize condemnation/sale of unsuitable materials and purchase of new supplies, an exchange may be effected provided net proceeds are covered into the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts (section 3618 R.S., as amended). Decisions C. 3414 and others provide procedures and conditions under which exchanges are lawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory mechanisms permit limited exchanges when proceeds covered to Treasury
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is statutory authority for condemnation/sale of unserviceable materials and statutory authority for purchase of new supplies, an exchange may be effected with part-payment credited and net proceeds covered into the Treasury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference to section 1241 R.S. and requirement that net proceeds of sale be 'covered into the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts' and appropriation for new supplies be charged for full value. Decisions: C. 3414 (various dates), 16 420, 20159.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary cannot sell or exchange military stores to States without authority
rubrics_metrics.description: In absence of statutory authority, the Secretary of War may not sell or exchange military stores in his possession to a State or similar government unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held prior to militia act of Jan. 21, 1903; later that act authorized certain sales/exchanges to States/Territories/District of Columbia for militia supplies. Decisions: P. 31, 497; 42, 371; C. 15286.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary furnishing of transportation or escort is not a 'loan' requiring congressional authority
rubrics_metrics.description: While loans of public property generally require congressional authority, temporarily furnishing transportation and an escort for a U.S. judge traveling to hold court has been held to be within the Secretary's discretion and not a loan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances where temporary furnishing was permitted: C. 228; 10655; 16155; 19282; 20846. Distinguish these discretionary, temporary uses from loans or permanent transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loans of public property generally unlawful without Congressional authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests to loan public property (tents, flags, dredges, etc.) have been, as a rule, denied on the ground that the Secretary of War lacks authority to loan government property unless authorized by act or resolution of Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some exceptions existed (dredges for navigation improvements), but practice generally requires congressional authorization. Cases: C. 1561; 2265; noted War Dept. actions in 1881 and 1895 as exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: President may use public property in emergencies to relieve suffering (necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: In certain emergencies the President has been held to be authorized to use United States property to relieve suffering among persons not otherwise entitled to such aid; such actions rest on necessity rather than specific statutory authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: issuance of rations to destitute persons in Alaskan districts; Acting Attorney General opinion (Oct. 15, 1908) treating emergency relief as permissible in absence of explicit statute; Secretary authorized issue of 10,000 rations for Texas flood sufferers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issuance of rations and relief measures are treated as acts of necessity, not statutory authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Issues of rations or temporary relief (e.g., to sufferers from flood/famine, or certain civilian patients) have been made on grounds of humanity/necessity despite lack of explicit statutory authority; they cannot be represented as having the force of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions C. 6836, 7493, 14347, 23289 and citations to Army Regulations paragraph 1241 sanction limited issues when commanding officer assumes responsibility to relieve starvation or extreme suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finder of government property does not acquire title absent abandonment or reward offer
rubrics_metrics.description: Sending government property into the field (e.g., a Signal Corps balloon) does not amount to abandonment; a finder who detains it is not entitled to keep it or to a lien for reward or expenses unless a reward was offered; appropriation by finder exposes civil and criminal liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case C. 18456: recommended referral to Attorney General to recover possession when a finder demanded $20 for return of balloon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfers of property between departments require authority and proper accounting; such transfers are not sales
rubrics_metrics.description: The transfer of public property from one bureau or department to another is not regarded as a sale but requires special authority (e.g., Secretary of War) and proper debit/crediting of appropriations; amount to be paid should include contract/invoice price and transportation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Army Regulations paragraphs 616 (630 of 1910) and 671 (682 of 1910) cited. Examples: transfers of clothing to Dept. of Justice for penitentiary prisoners; transfers of mules between appropriations when authorized and accounted for. Decisions: C. 3679, 7184, 11839, 12191, 12491, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exchange or transfer of reservations between departments requires Congressional authority unless temporary license pending Congressional action
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete exchange or transfer of reservation lands between departments (e.g., lighthouse for military reservation) would not be legal without Congress; however, departments may grant licenses to occupy lands of another department pending action by Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opinions C. 3657, 8743, 11478; examples of transfers by President (Dry Tortugas to Navy) where reservation was reserved from public domain and President directed transfer; caution where purchased land (not reserved) requires Congressional authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of donations of property is permissible absent statute forbidding it
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of a statute forbidding acceptance (analogous to restrictions on purchase of land or voluntary services), the government may accept donations of property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: acceptance of six horses (C. 27872) and donation of shell for road repair by county (C. 29257) where donation benefitted both community and government; but special statutes govern donations of land in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary cannot accept gift of land or easement except with statutory authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Under section 3736 R.S. ('no land shall be purchased on account of the United States except under a law authorizing such purchase'), a head of department cannot accept a grant by gift of land or an easement in land without statutory authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions: R. 32, 19; 38, 175; 39, 313; 44, 9; C. 3896, 11024, 12702, 13854, 13586. The term 'purchase' is construed broadly to include acquisition other than by descent, so acceptance of a gift can be barred absent authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation funds cannot be expended for building on donated land until title approved and state consent given
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where land is donated, public money legally cannot be expended to erect public buildings on that donated land until the Attorney General approves the title and the state's legislature consents to the grant (where required).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advised in R. 32, 19 and related authorities; emphasizes procedural prerequisites before expenditures on donated lands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory authority to purchase land must be clear and indisputable
rubrics_metrics.description: A head of department's power to purchase land requires clear, indisputable statutory authority; general appropriations or vague wording (e.g., 'establishment' of a post) are insufficient where specific prohibitions exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: authority to purchase additional cemetery land could not be derived from a general appropriation to maintain existing cemeteries (R. 44, 50); C. 12154 regarding Manila. Statutes conferring specific purchase power are to be strictly construed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific land-purchase statutes are strictly construed and must be complied with in terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a statute authorizes purchase of a described tract for a stated sum and acreage, the officer has no discretion to purchase only a portion or vary the terms; the statutory description and terms must be strictly followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions: R. 38, 346; P. 37, 203; C. 13580, 15110, 24464. But implied authority (e.g., sec. 1838 R.S. for fort sites) may operate in limited contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custody confers responsibility and accountability for government property
rubrics_metrics.description: Any officer who has the custody of Government property is responsible for it, regardless of where accountability might otherwise rest on paper; absence of a receipt for an item does not excuse failure to exercise utmost diligence to safeguard it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General principle: officers are liable only where a loss resulted from failure to exercise the degree of care circumstances required. Decision: C. 27780 and P. 46,340.

rubrics_metrics.name: When an officer is permanently relieved, responsibility for property devolves to successor (absent exigency)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an officer is permanently relieved and another is placed in command, responsibility and accountability for company property should devolve upon the successor, with proper receipts taken; the relieved officer should not be required to retain responsibility after permanent relief unless exigencies prevented formal transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case C. 27780 (Feb. 4, 1911) — outlines expectations for formal transfer and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board of survey (surveying officer) powers and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A board of survey is not a court and cannot exercise powers expressly vested in courts-martial or courts of inquiry; it cannot convict of crime or impose criminal penalties, and its opinions about theft cannot be treated as judicial findings to stop a soldier's pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R. 34, 306; R. 42, 605 cited. Boards may prepare reports and fix pecuniary responsibility but cannot legally determine criminal guilt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boards of survey may not administer oaths but may receive affidavits
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no statute or regulation authorizing a board of survey to be sworn or to swear witnesses; however, boards may receive and file affidavits of persons cognizant of facts under investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: B. 5, 590; R. V, 590; citations to Army Regulations and later statutory provisions (e.g., sec. 183 R.S. as amended) that affect investigatory oath authority in other contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officer who pays on forged vouchers is legally accountable; permitting access may be military offense enforceable by court-martial
rubrics_metrics.description: If a disbursing officer pays money of the United States on forged transportation requests, he is legally accountable for the loss; an officer who allowed access to blank forms may be subject to military discipline, but pecuniary accountability rests with the disbursing officer who paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by corporal forging requests and disbursing officer paying them: P. 56, 208; Comptroller decisions discussing railroad good-faith acceptance and company entitlement to payment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gratuitous bailee standard for custody of government property
rubrics_metrics.description: A person acting as a gratuitous bailee (e.g., officer entrusted with a Medal of Honor for delivery) is required only to the lowest degree of care and is not liable for loss unless the loss resulted from gross negligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case P. 44, 382 (Dec., 1890) — officer locked medal in trunk for transport and held not legally accountable; distinguishes degrees of care for bailees.
